## Herbs: plant knowledge before correspondence


Herbs can enter a ritual through folklore, foodways, household medicine, devotional practice, scent, season, or local ecology. A chart that gives each plant one word hides most of that history.


Rosemary offers a familiar example. In *Hamlet* , Ophelia says, “[There’s rosemary, that’s for remembrance](https://www.folger.edu/explore/shakespeares-works/hamlet/read/4/5/) .” The line, preserved in the Folger Shakespeare Library edition, shows the association in early modern English literature. It doesn’t establish the origin of rosemary magick or make remembrance the plant’s sole meaning. A practitioner might choose rosemary through literature, Mediterranean folk custom, a family kitchen, or a modern correspondence book.


Lavender can arrive through a scent association or a household custom. A modern book may assign it a word, but that entry needs a name and source before it joins your practice. Garden sage may be chosen from a local plant bed. Name which path brought the herb to your altar. “Traditional” without a people, place, text, or teacher attached tells the reader very little.


### White sage calls for more specific care


The California Native Plant Society’s[White Sage Protection project](https://www.cnps.org/conservation/white-sage) , created with Rose Ramirez and Deborah Small and featuring named Indigenous contributors, identifies white sage as *Salvia apiana* . The project describes its deep relationships with Indigenous communities of Southern California and northern Baja and documents commercial poaching.


A generic instruction to “burn sage for cleansing” erases those relationships. Learn which plant you have, ask how it was grown or gathered, and seek nation-specific teaching rather than treating all Indigenous practice as one voice. Garden-grown rosemary, lavender, or another plant from your own tradition may fit the ritual without borrowing a rite you have not been taught.


**Natural is not the same as safe.** Don’t ingest an altar herb or apply an oil because a correspondence chart calls it natural. Poison Control warns that[essential oils can cause rashes or poisoning when misused](https://www.poison.org/articles/essential-oils) and advises following labels and keeping oils away from children and pets.
